A.explanation: This subtracts the initial $5 \text{ kJ}$ instead of adding it, giving $50 - 10 - 5 = 35 \text{ kJ}$.

B.explanation: The $50 \text{ kJ}$ loss of potential energy plus the initial $5 \text{ kJ}$ of kinetic energy minus $10 \text{ kJ}$ lost to friction gives $45 \text{ kJ}$.

C.explanation: This adds $5 \text{ kJ}$ to $50 \text{ kJ}$ but ignores the $10 \text{ kJ}$ of work done against friction.

hints: Notice the three energies in kJ: $5 \text{ kJ}$ kinetic energy at P, $50 \text{ kJ}$ drop in potential energy from P to Q, and $10 \text{ kJ}$ of work against friction.
Recall that lost potential energy becomes available, but work against friction removes energy from the kinetic plus potential store: $KE_P + PE_P = KE_Q + PE_Q + W_{friction}$.
Add the released $50 \text{ kJ}$ to the starting $5 \text{ kJ}$, then subtract the $10 \text{ kJ}$ lost to friction to find $KE_Q$.
walkthrough: Write the energy conservation including friction: initial total at P equals final total at Q plus energy lost. So $KE_P + PE_P = KE_Q + PE_Q + W_{friction}$.
Rearrange for the wanted kinetic energy at Q: $KE_Q = KE_P + (PE_P - PE_Q) - W_{friction}$.
Identify the potential energy released: $PE_P - PE_Q = 50 \text{ kJ}$ because potential energy at Q is $50 \text{ kJ}$ less than at P.
Substitute with units: $KE_Q = 5 \text{ kJ} + 50 \text{ kJ} - 10 \text{ kJ}$.
Calculate: $5 + 50 = 55 \text{ kJ}$ of available energy, then $55 - 10 = 45 \text{ kJ}$ remains as kinetic energy at Q.
